How to split a single address block into several smaller networks by taking bits from the host part, how to compute ranges, broadcast and mask, and how to allocate tailored blocks with VLSM without waste.

A single block and a new branch office

We have two stations on a hub, a router and the segment 200.1.10.0/24 that IANA assigned to us: all our addresses start with the prefix 200.1.10.

We open a branch office and want it to be a different network. There are two options:

  • Ask IANA for another segment: hard, because segments are limited.
  • Use subnets: take the segment we already have and split it into smaller networks.
A subnet is a piece of the original block that works as a separate network.
Taking host bits for the subnet

With /24, the first three octets are network and the last one (8 bits) is host.

The idea is to take bits from that octet (lock them) to identify the subnet and leave the rest for the hosts. With the first 2 bits there are four combinations: 00, 01, 10 and 11 → 4 subnets.

The cost: the more bits are taken, the fewer hosts fit in each one. 6 bits remain: 2⁶ = 64 addresses, minus the network and broadcast addresses = 62 hosts.
Each bit that moves from host to subnet doubles the subnets and halves their size.

In each subnet, the first address (host all 0s) identifies the subnet and the last (host all 1s) is its broadcast.

Example: 200.1.10.130. Its last octet is 10000010: it starts with 10, so it belongs to 200.1.10.128/26, with hosts from .129 to .190 and broadcast .191.

The mask has 24 + 2 = 26 ones: 11000000 = 192 → 255.255.255.192.

The broadcast of the last subnet is .255, the same as that of the original network: today that is not a problem.
Subnet = first address of the block · broadcast = last · hosts = everything in between.
Address .130 falls in the third subnet

We open two more branch offices: now there are 5. With two bits we only had four combinations, so we have to take one more bit.

With 3 fixed bits there are 2³ = 8 combinations (enough for the 5, with 3 left over).

That leaves 5 bits for hosts: 2⁵ − 2 = 30 hosts per subnet.

The mask becomes /27: 11100000 = 224 → 255.255.255.224.
More subnets = fewer hosts in each: we went from 62 down to 30.
Last octet: eight /27 subnets of 32 addresses (5 in use)
Third case: subnets of different sizes

Now we want a headquarters with a large set of addresses, and another set for the rest.

We use the first bit of the last octet to split into two /25 halves. The one starting with 0 is kept for the headquarters (hosts .1 to .126).

The one starting with 1 keeps being divided: fixing one more bit gives 10 and 11, two /26 subnets starting at .128 and at .192 (128 + 64).
Not all subnets need to be the same size: you can keep splitting just one half.
The second half splits into two /26
Rule of thumb: divide 256 and subtract 2

To know how many addresses each subnet has, keep dividing 256: with 2 subnets it is 128 each; if one is split, 64; then 32, 16…

From each block you subtract 2 (the subnet address and the broadcast): 126, 62, 30, 14…

The next subnet starts where the previous one ends: 128 + 64 = 192.

For the mask, count the fixed bits: 24 → 255.255.255.0; each extra bit adds its weight to the last octet (128, 192, 224, 240…).
Block size = 256 divided by the number of subnets. Hosts = size − 2.
Each fixed bit halves the block

New requirement: a subnet of 10 hosts and another of 2 hosts. If we give each one a /26 (62 hosts), we are wasting addresses.

The idea of VLSM is similar to IANA's classes: blocks of different sizes, tailored.

  • 10 hosts: you need 4 bits of host (2⁴ − 2 = 14). That leaves 4 subnet bits → /28.
  • 2 hosts: 2 bits are enough (2² − 2 = 2) → /30.
Choose the fewest host bits that cover the requirement; the rest of the octet is subnet.
Without VLSM: two /26 for 10 and 2 hosts
Reserve one chunk and divide the other

The method is iterative: from each block you reserve one half for future use and divide the other, until reaching the requested size.

  • .128/26 is kept in reserve; .192/26 is split into two /27.
  • .192/27 in reserve; .224/27 is split into two /28.
  • .224/28 (14 usable) → the 10-host subnet.
  • .240/28 is split: .240/29 in reserve and, inside .248, the .248/30 → the 2-host one.

In the figure in the notes, it gets the whole /29 (6 usable).
Large blocks in reserve, small blocks tailored: that leaves room to grow.
Zoom on end of block (224 to 255): .248/30 is the 2-host subnet
Growing: only adjacent chunks can be merged

Having split so much has a problem: what if a subnet needs more hosts?

Chunks can be merged, that is, build a larger one from two smaller ones, but only if they are contiguous.

That is why it pays to leave a whole contiguous chunk in reserve next to each subnet, and always to split in a way that lets you merge again later. It is not always possible to reserve everything contiguously: do it as much as you can.
Two contiguous halves form the block they came from again, with one less prefix bit.
If it grows again, absorbs adjacent reserve
Subnets and VLSM at a glance

• Subnet: bits are taken from the host part to identify it. n bits → 2ⁿ subnets.
  • Usable hosts = 2 to the number of host bits, minus 2 (subnet and broadcast).
  • Rule of thumb: divide 256 and subtract 2. The next subnet starts by adding the size.
  • Mask = number of fixed bits: /26 → .192, /27 → .224, /28 → .240.
  • VLSM: tailored blocks, reserving contiguous ones to grow.

We now know which IP each host has and which network it belongs to. One detail is missing: to deliver a frame to a neighbor we need its MAC. ARP solves that.
200.1.10.0/24 is divided into 4 equal subnets. Which one does host 200.1.10.100 belong to, and what is that subnet's broadcast?
100 = 01100100 starts with 01: it is subnet .64/26, which runs from .64 to .127 (hosts .65 – .126, broadcast .127).
5 equal subnets are needed inside a /24. What prefix, mask and number of hosts per subnet result?
For 5 subnets you need 3 bits (8 combinations): /27, mask .224. 5 host bits remain: 2⁵ − 2 = 30.
With VLSM you must place a 10-host subnet and a 2-host one. Which prefixes fit without waste?
10 hosts need 4 host bits (2⁴ − 2 = 14) → /28; 2 hosts need 2 bits (2² − 2 = 2) → /30. A /29 only gives 6 hosts.
Subnet 200.1.10.128/25 is split in two. What are the resulting subnets?
Fixing one more bit divides the 128 block into two of 64: the first starts at .128 and the second at 128 + 64 = .192.
Bits are taken from the host part to identify it: n bits → 2ⁿ subnets, each with fewer hosts.
2 to the number of host bits, minus 2: the first address is the subnet and the last is the broadcast.
3 subnet bits → 8 subnets of 30 hosts · mask 255.255.255.224.
Divide 256: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4… and subtract 2. Next subnet = previous + size.
Subnets of different sizes according to need: 10 hosts → /28 (14), 2 hosts → /30 (2).
Reserve one half, divide the other. Only contiguous chunks can be merged.
